title: sentence structure — word order
explanation: Basic Japanese sentence order: subject(wa) → time(ni) → place(de) → object(wo) → verb(-masu). Not every part is needed in every sentence — Japanese drops whatever is already clear from context.
example: わたしは 3じに レストランで ピザを たべます。
exampleMeaning: I eat pizza at the restaurant at 3 o'clock. (subject–time–place–object–verb)

title: は — wa (topic marker)
explanation: は marks the sentence's topic — what the sentence is about. Written は but pronounced 'wa' when used as this particle.
example: わたしは がくせいです。
exampleMeaning: As for me, I'm a student.

title: に — ni (time / direction marker)
explanation: に marks a point in time ('at/on') or a destination ('to'). Comes right after the time word or the place being moved toward. Exception: relative time words like ima (now) never take に.
example: 7じに おきます。がっこうに いきます。
exampleMeaning: I wake up at 7. I go to school.

title: で — de (place / means marker)
explanation: で marks where an action happens ('at/in') or the means/tool used to do it ('by/with').
example: こうえんで あそびます。バスで いきます。
exampleMeaning: I play at the park. I go by bus.

title: を — wo -  direct-object particle
explanation: を (pronounced 'o') marks the direct object: the thing the verb acts on. It comes right before the verb.

title: Ru-verb → ます
explanation: For ru-verbs, drop the final -ru and add -masu.
example: たべる → たべます。わたしは たべます。

title: U-verb → ます
explanation: For u-verbs, change the final u-row sound to the matching i-row sound, then add -masu. Kaeru is an exeption and is a U-verb
example: きく → ききます。ホンダさんは のみます。
exampleMeaning: to listen/ask → (I) listen. Mr. Honda drinks. (kiku → kikimasu, nomu → nomimasu)

title: irregular verbs — する / くる
explanation: suru (to do) and kuru (to come) don't follow the ru-verb or u-verb pattern: suru → shimasu, kuru → kimasu. Very common since many verbs are noun + suru (benkyou suru = to study).
example: にほんじんは べんきょうします。
exampleMeaning: The Japanese person studies. (benkyou suru → benkyou shimasu)

title: か — question marker
explanation: Put か at the end of a sentence to turn it into a yes/no question. No change in word order, and often no question mark is needed.

title: の — linking nouns / possession
explanation: の joins two nouns: A の B means 'B of A' or 'A's B'. The owner or describer comes first.
example: わたしの ほん。にほんの くるま。

title: kore / sore / are & kono / sono / ano — 'this / that'
explanation: kore, sore, are stand alone as 'this one / that one / that one over there', by distance from speaker and listener. kono, sono, ano cover the same three distances but must be followed directly by a noun — they never stand alone.
example: これは わたしの ペンです。このノートは 100えんです。
exampleMeaning: This is my pen. This notebook is 100 yen.

title: Japanglish — how foreign sounds shift
explanation: Japanese phonology forces a few systematic swaps when borrowing foreign words: v→b, r/l→r (no separate l sound), si→shi, zi→ji.

title: じん (jin) — nationality suffix
explanation: Add じん (jin) right after a country name to mean 'a person from that country'.

title: הטיות — です (שמות עצם)
explanation: How です (the copula, used after nouns/な-adjectives) conjugates for tense and polarity.
